title: Talking and communicating
subtitle: talk shop, get to the point, speak your mind
summary: Learn the idioms English uses for good talk, bad talk and communication that goes wrong - from talking at cross-purposes to putting it in a nutshell.

lesson.heading: When communication goes wrong
rows: talk about different things without realising it
get (hold of) the wrong end of the stick
not understand something in the correct way
can't get a word in edgeways
get no chance to speak because others are talking so much
can't make head or tail of something

lesson.heading: Communication problems in action
lesson.text: These idioms describe very common everyday situations. Notice that **get a word in edgeways** and **make head or tail of** are almost always used in the negative.

examples.text: *Paul:* Ninety-eight pounds for a meal! *Emma:* Not the meal, you idiot! The room! - They were **talking at cross-purposes**.
He thought she was in love with him; she had only said she liked him as a friend. He'd **got the wrong end of the stick**.
Everyone was talking at once, so poor Meena **couldn't get a word in edgeways**.
It was full of legal language and provisos - I **couldn't make head or tail of** it.

lesson.heading: Good talk, bad talk
rows: talk as if they were inferior
say negative things when they are not there
a subject everyone wants to talk about
reproach or scold someone, tell them off

lesson.heading: Good talk, bad talk in sentences
lesson.text: Most of these expressions carry a judgment - usually a negative one. **Small talk** is neutral, but the others are almost always a complaint.

examples.text: The boss always **talks down to** us, as if we knew nothing.
My workmates are always **talking behind my back**.
It was just **small talk**, nothing more, I promise.
Let's sit somewhere else; they always **talk shop** over lunch, and it bores me rigid.
Your new friend's become a real **talking point** among the staff!
It's gone too far this time. I shall have to **give him a talking to**.

lesson.heading: Talk in discussions and meetings
rows: say it in very few words
get to / come to the point
reach the important part of the matter
say things in a long, indirect way

lesson.heading: Using the meeting idioms
lesson.text: These are the phrases you hear again and again in meetings and debates. **Long-winded** is an adjective; the rest are verb phrases.

examples.text: Who's going to **start the ball rolling**?
**To put it in a nutshell**, this is a waste of time.
I hope they **get to the point** soon.
I want to **speak my mind** today.
I hope we **wrap up** the discussion by 12.30.

lesson.text: Learn *talk sense* and *talk rubbish* as a pair, and *talk shop*, *small talk* and *a talking point* as a family - you will remember them far better together than one by one.

exercises.prompt: Match each idiom with its meaning.

pairs.right: talk about different things without realising it

pairs.left: get the wrong end of the stick
can't get a word in edgeways
can't make head or tail of it

pairs.right: talk as if they were inferior
say things in a long, indirect way

exercises.prompt: Meena kept starting to say something, but the others never stopped. She couldn't get a word in ___.
exercises.explanation: To not get a word in edgeways is to have no chance to speak because others talk so much.

exercises.prompt: Ali said he didn't expect someone with Juan's intelligence to understand the document. Ali was talking ___ to Juan.
exercises.explanation: To talk down to someone is to talk as if they were inferior.

exercises.prompt: Volodya got upset because he thought Gina had called him childish; in fact she hadn't. He got the ___ of the stick.
exercises.explanation: To get (hold of) the wrong end of the stick is to understand something incorrectly.

exercises.prompt: Dan's report was full of jargon like 'down-matching sales profile commitment'. Kim couldn't make head or ___ of it.
exercises.explanation: To not make head or tail of something is to fail to understand it at all.

exercises.prompt: She is very direct and always speaks her ___.
exercises.explanation: To speak your mind is to say exactly what you think.

exercises.prompt: He gets bored quickly with small ___ and always wants to get down to serious matters.
exercises.explanation: Small talk is purely social conversation with nothing serious in it.

exercises.prompt: You're behind the times! George's girlfriend was last week's talking ___.
exercises.explanation: A talking point is a subject everyone wants to talk about.

exercises.prompt: I hate going out with my boyfriend and his work colleagues - they spend all evening talking ___.
exercises.explanation: To talk shop is to talk about work when you are not at work.

exercises.prompt: You should tell him what you think to his face rather than talking behind his ___.
exercises.explanation: To talk behind someone's back is to say negative things when they are absent.

exercises.prompt: The boss gave me a real ___ to after that stupid mistake I made.
exercises.explanation: To give someone a talking to is to reproach or scold them.

exercises.prompt: Paula's uncle takes ten minutes to make a point anyone else could make in 30 seconds. He is very ___.
exercises.explanation: Long-winded means saying things in a long, indirect way.

exercises.prompt: Does each expression describe good talk or bad talk?
Put this meeting sentence in order.
exercises.answer: Who's going to start the ball rolling?
exercises.explanation: To start the ball rolling is to begin the discussion.

exercises.statement: It was such a relief when James got up to speak - at last someone was talking sense.
exercises.explanation: Correct - to talk sense is to say intelligent, reasonable things.
